title: Understanding Ratios
subject: Math
unitTitle: Unit 1: Ratios, Rates, and Proportional Reasoning
developmentNotes: Grade 6 students often treat ratios as subtraction or isolated fractions. Emphasize relationship between two quantities and multiple equivalent representations.
learningObjective: Students will describe ratios as relationships between quantities, write ratios in multiple forms, and use ratio reasoning to solve contextual problems.
essentialQuestion: How can one relationship describe two quantities at the same time?

vocabularyTerms.definition: a ratio that describes the same relationship using different numbers
a comparison between one part and the total
a ratio comparing quantities with different units

prerequisites: Compare quantities using words and numbers

hook.content: A trail mix has 2 cups of raisins for every 3 cups of nuts. Students decide whether a batch with 4 cups raisins and 6 cups nuts tastes the same, stronger, or weaker.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

learningGoal.content: I can students will describe ratios as relationships between quantities, write ratios in multiple forms, and use ratio reasoning to solve contextual problems.
successCriteria: I can explain the core concept in my own words.
I can show evidence or reasoning, not only an answer.
I can correct a common mistake.

miniTeach.content: A ratio compares quantities. The order matters because 2 raisins to 3 nuts is not the same statement as 3 raisins to 2 nuts. Ratios can be written as 2 to 3, 2:3, or 2/3 when comparing raisins to nuts. Equivalent ratios keep the same relationship.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.coreConcept: A ratio is a relationship between quantities.
known: The mix has 2 cups raisins for every 3 cups nuts.
The relationship matters more than the raw size of the batch.
unknown: Whether another pair of quantities preserves the same relationship.
rules: Multiply or divide both quantities by the same factor to make an equivalent ratio.
Ratio order must match the meaning.
Part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons answer different questions.
avoid: Do not subtract quantities to compare ratio relationships.
Do not reverse the ratio without changing the meaning.
steps: Scale both parts by the same factor.
Check whether the relationship stayed constant.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: For 2:3 and 4:6, both parts doubled, so the relationship stayed the same.

workedExample.content: Problem: There are 6 red tiles and 9 blue tiles. Ratio red to blue is 6:9. Divide both by 3 to simplify to 2:3. Equivalent examples include 4:6 and 8:12.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Write three forms of the ratio 5 dogs to 2 cats.
Identify whether 3:4 is part-to-part or part-to-whole in a class with 3 sixth graders and 4 seventh graders.
Scale 2:5 by 3 and explain the result.
Debug: A student says 2:3 and 4:5 are equivalent because both increased by 2.
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

reteachPath.misconception: Student uses additive comparison instead of multiplicative ratio reasoning.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: Equivalent ratios keep the same relationship by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number.
steps: Multiply both parts by the same factor.
Check with a table or double number line.

practice.answer: Not equivalent; scale by multiplication instead.

practice.prompt: Part-to-whole in 2 red and 3 blue: red to total

successCriteria: I can explain what both quantities in a ratio mean.
I can build equivalent ratios by scaling both quantities together.
I can use a table or double number line to find a unit rate.
I can defend which deal is better with evidence.

knowledge: A ratio compares two quantities in a chosen order.
A unit rate compares a quantity to one unit.
capability: Build a ratio table and double number line.
Compare real-world deals with unit rates.
reasoning: Detect additive scaling and total-price traps.
retention: Recall the equivalent-ratio rule after a delay.
transfer: Apply ratio reasoning to recipes, maps, budgets, or game currency.

phaseModules.title: Enter the neon market
phaseModules.studentAction: Choose which deal looks better and write what evidence you need to prove it.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name the comparison I need to make.

phaseModules.title: See the relationship
phaseModules.studentAction: Watch a ratio table and double number line show the same relationship before using a shortcut.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can match a table row to a point on the number line.

phaseModules.title: Label and scale
phaseModules.studentAction: Separate quantity labels, scale factor, equivalent ratio, and unit rate in a worked deal.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain what every number represents.

phaseModules.title: Build the better-deal board
phaseModules.studentAction: Complete two ratio tables, map them, and calculate both unit rates.
phaseModules.successCheck: My representations and unit-rate sentences agree.

phaseModules.title: Defend the fair comparison
phaseModules.studentAction: Use because and two labeled unit rates to defend which deal is better.
phaseModules.successCheck: I do not choose from total price alone.

phaseModules.title: Complete the checkpoint
phaseModules.studentAction: Answer the ratio and rate questions independently and explain one choice.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can show the reasoning without a final-answer hint.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the comparison rule
phaseModules.studentAction: Return later and recall how equivalent ratios and unit rates make comparisons fair.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve the rule without the original diagram.

phaseModules.title: Find a real better deal
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply the method to a new recipe, map, price, or classroom-budget problem.
phaseModules.successCheck: The method works when the story changes.

phaseModules.title: Choose reteach or challenge
phaseModules.studentAction: Repair labels or scaling when evidence shows a gap, or design a misleading deal when secure.
phaseModules.successCheck: My next move matches the error evidence.

proofTasks.prompt: State the rule for creating an equivalent ratio.
Explain why adding the same number can change a ratio relationship.

Solve a new unit-rate comparison after a delay.

feedbackRules.result: The learner changes the meaning by reversing quantity order.
feedbackRules.hint: Label both quantities before writing the ratio.
feedbackRules.action: Return to the first labeled row.

feedbackRules.result: The learner adds instead of using a shared scale factor.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask what number multiplies both quantities.

feedbackRules.result: The learner chooses by total price instead of cost per unit.
feedbackRules.hint: Reduce both deals to one unit.
feedbackRules.action: Retry with the unit-rate sentence frame.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner cannot explain what the two numbers mean.
reteachPaths.action: Use labeled item cards, then build two equivalent table rows.

reteachPaths.trigger: The learner compares totals instead of unit rates.
reteachPaths.action: Find the cost for one item in each deal before choosing.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot divide the quantities.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair whole-number and decimal division with a simpler price example.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner compares unit rates independently.
challengePaths.action: Design a deal that looks cheaper but has a worse unit rate.

parentTeacherNotes: When cooking or mixing drinks, ask the student to explain how changing one ingredient affects the ratio.
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
